content: Lichen planus is a chronic inflammatory condition that primarily affects the skin and mucous membranes, including the oral cavity. It is characterized by distinct clinical features and histopathological findings. Overview Lichen planus is an immune-mediated inflammatory disease that targets the skin, oral mucosa, and occasionally other mucosal surfaces. It is marked by the presence of pruritic, violaceous, polygonal papules and plaques on the skin, as well as reticular white streaks (Wickham's striae) on the mucosa. The condition can be chronic and relapsing, with variable severity. Classification When lichen planus involves the scalp, it is referred to as lichen planopilaris. This variant can lead to permanent scarring alopecia if left untreated. The scarring process results in irreversible hair loss. Organizations such as the Cicatricial Alopecia Research Foundation provide resources and support for individuals affected by this condition. Pathophysiology and Causes The exact etiology of lichen planus remains unknown, but it is believed to involve an autoimmune mechanism where T-cells target basal keratinocytes. Several factors have been implicated in its development: 1. Drug-induced lichenoid reactions: Certain medications, such as antihypertensives (e.g., hydrochlorothiazide, methyldopa), antimalarials (e.g., chloroquine, mepacrine), gold salts, and penicillamine, can trigger lichenoid eruptions resembling lichen planus. 2. Infectious associations: Chronic hepatitis C virus infection has been linked to lichen planus, particularly in cases involving the oral mucosa. 3. Graft-versus-host disease: Lichen planus-like lesions may occur as a manifestation of chronic graft-versus-host disease. 4. Stress: Psychological stress has been suggested as a potential trigger for disease flares in susceptible individuals. Clinical Presentation Skin Lesions The hallmark of lichen planus is the 5 P's: pruritic, planar, purple, polygonal papules. These lesions are often symmetrically distributed and commonly involve the flexor surfaces of the wrists, ankles, and lower back. Over time, the lesions may heal with post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, leaving blue-black or brownish discoloration. Oral Lesions Oral lichen planus can present in three distinct forms: Reticular form: The most common presentation, characterized by white, lacy streaks (Wickham's striae) on the buccal mucosa, tongue, or gingiva. These lesions are typically asymptomatic. Erosive form: This form is associated with painful, erythematous, and ulcerated areas, often accompanied by Wickham's striae at the periphery. It carries a risk of malignant transformation into oral squamous cell carcinoma. Bullous form: Rarely, fluid-filled vesicles may develop, which can rupture and leave erosions. Genital and Esophageal Involvement Lichen planus can affect the genital mucosa, presenting as vulvovaginal-gingival syndrome in women or penile lesions in men. Esophageal involvement, though rare, may manifest as erosive esophagitis or strictures and has been hypothesized to predispose to esophageal squamous cell carcinoma. Nail and Hair Involvement Nail changes, such as pitting, ridging, or onycholysis, may occur. In severe cases, nail loss can result. Scalp involvement (lichen planopilaris) leads to cicatricial alopecia, characterized by permanent hair loss due to follicular destruction. Diagnosis The diagnosis of lichen planus is primarily clinical, supported by histopathological findings on biopsy. Key microscopic features include: Hyperparakeratosis with thickening of the granular cell layer. A saw-tooth appearance of the rete ridges. Degeneration of the basal cell layer. Band-like infiltration of lymphocytes in the subepithelial connective tissue. Differential diagnoses include lichenoid drug reactions, discoid lupus erythematosus, chronic ulcerative stomatitis, pemphigus vulgaris, and oral leukoplakia. A biopsy is essential to confirm the diagnosis and exclude other conditions. Epidemiology Lichen planus is most commonly observed in middle-aged adults, with a female predominance (3:2 ratio). It is rare in children. Natural History and Complications Lichen planus is generally a self-limiting condition, with most cases resolving within 18 months. However, it may persist for years with intermittent flares. Chronic oral lesions, particularly the erosive form, carry a risk of malignant transformation into oral squamous cell carcinoma. Other complications include scarring alopecia and esophageal strictures. Treatment There is no definitive cure for lichen planus, but treatment aims to control symptoms and reduce inflammation. Therapeutic options include: 1. Topical and systemic corticosteroids: These are the mainstay of treatment for both cutaneous and mucosal lesions. 2. Immunomodulators: Tacrolimus and pimecrolimus are used for refractory cases, particularly in mucosal involvement. 3. Oral retinoids: Acitretin may be effective in severe or widespread disease. 4. Hydroxychloroquine: This antimalarial agent is sometimes used for lichen planopilaris. 5. Dapsone: An anti-inflammatory agent that may benefit certain patients. 6. Immunosuppressants: Agents such as methotrexate or mycophenolate mofetil are reserved for severe, refractory cases. Prognosis With appropriate treatment, most cases of lichen planus can be managed effectively. However, the disease may recur after periods of remission. Long-term follow-up is recommended for patients with oral or esophageal involvement due to the risk of malignant transformation. Avoidance of known triggers, such as certain medications and stress, may help reduce the risk of flares in susceptible individuals. Regular monitoring and early intervention are crucial for managing complications.
